summary: KS3 pupils learn to identify, describe and perform the three rigid plane transformations — translation, reflection and rotation — treating them as one family that produces a CONGRUENT image (same lengths and angles) and differs only in effect on position, orientation and 'sense' (handedness). The core teaching moves: insist every transformation be fully specified by its defining data (translation = column vector; reflection = equation of mirror line; rotation = centre + angle + direction), use sense (whether the shape is flipped) as the test separating reflection from rotation, treat the mirror line as the perpendicular bisector of each point→image segment, and extend beyond horizontal/vertical mirrors to diagonal mirrors (y=x, y=−x) and off-shape rotation centres. A clearly-handed scalene shape (an 'F' or a flag) on a four-quadrant grid makes a flipped vs unflipped image visible at a glance.
misconceptions: Reflecting in a diagonal mirror but keeping the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane (overuse of H/V mirrors)
Confusing rotation and reflection because sense is never checked
Describing a rotation without its centre or direction, or assuming clockwise
Swapping x and y when reading or writing image coordinates (reversal) carried into the image
Thinking a rigid transformation can change the size of the shape

activities.title: Reflect, then try to copy it with a rotation
steps: On a four-quadrant coordinate grid, take a scalene, obviously-handed shape (an 'F' or a flag) and reflect it in the line y=x, recording the image coordinates of each vertex (e.g. (1,4) maps to (4,1) — for y=x, swap the coordinates).

For each vertex not lying on the mirror line, draw the segment from the point to its image and check it meets the mirror line at a right angle, crossing at the midpoint — confirming the mirror is the perpendicular bisector of every such point→image segment (a vertex on y=x maps to itself, so it has no segment).
Note whether the shape's handedness has changed: for the reflection the 'F' should appear mirror-imaged.

Now try to land the ORIGINAL shape on top of your reflected image using a ROTATION instead: pin a centre, choose 90° clockwise, and compare. Observe that the rotated shape keeps its handedness and so cannot coincide with the flipped reflection.
State in your own words why reflection and rotation give different results here: one reverses sense (handedness), the other preserves it.
activities.insight: Reflection reverses sense while rotation and translation preserve it; this handedness test is what distinguishes a reflection from a rotation even when the image lands in a similar place. Reflecting in y=x swaps the x and y coordinates (reflection in y=−x swaps and negates them: (x,y)→(−y,−x)), not merely slides the shape across.

activities.title: Fully describe a rotation — centre, angle and direction
steps: Rotate the original shape 90° clockwise about the point (0,0) and describe exactly what you did, naming the centre, the angle AND the direction (clockwise/anticlockwise).
Check that your description is complete enough for someone else to reproduce the image uniquely: 'a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin'.
Carry out two 90° rotations of the same shape about two different centres and compare where the image lands, to feel why the centre is essential and not optional.
Given only an object and its image, reconstruct the centre of rotation by joining two or more object points to their images and intersecting the perpendicular bisectors of those segments.
activities.insight: A rotation is not fully described — and cannot be uniquely reproduced — without its centre, angle and direction (direction can only be left out for a 180° turn, where both directions give the same image). The centre genuinely changes where the image lands, and can be found by construction.

activities.title: Translate and prove congruence
steps: Translate the original shape by the column vector with top entry 4 and bottom entry −3, i.e. 4 right, 3 down (shift every vertex +4 in x and −3 in y), writing the image coordinates.
State whether the lengths and angles have changed, and explain how you know: because the transformation is rigid, the image is congruent to the object.
Prove congruence rather than assume it — trace the object on tracing paper and lay it over the image, or measure corresponding sides and angles, confirming they match.
Record every coordinate as x before y ('along the corridor then up the stairs') to avoid reversing the pair.
activities.insight: All three transformations are rigid motions: they preserve length and angle, so the image is always congruent to the object. Congruence should be checked, not taken on trust. Coordinates are written x before y.

activities.title: Identify and describe the transformation from object and image
steps: Given an object A and an image B, name which single transformation maps A to B and describe it with its full data set (vector, or mirror line, or centre+angle+direction).
Use sense first: decide whether the shape has been flipped. If flipped, it is a reflection; if not, it is a rotation or translation.
Guard against a tempting wrong answer: an image in the 'right place' but with reversed handedness is a reflection, NOT a rotation, even if a rotation seems to put it roughly there.

Pair several object→image cases with the correct transformation, and for any rotation make sure you have supplied the centre, the angle and (unless the angle is 180°) the direction before accepting the description as complete.
activities.insight: Describing a transformation is the reverse task of performing one: checking sense immediately narrows the family, and a rotation's description is incomplete until the centre, the angle and (except for 180°) the direction are given.

activities.title: Pre-teach the vocabulary with a labelled diagram
steps: On a labelled diagram of an object and its image, point to the mirror line and name it: 'the perpendicular bisector of each point-to-image line'.
Point to the image and name its relationship to the object: 'congruent to the object — same lengths and angles'.
Match each transformation to the data that defines it: translation→vector; reflection→mirror line; rotation→centre, angle and direction.
Use this only to fix terms, then move on to actually performing and checking a transformation.
activities.insight: The precise vocabulary — perpendicular bisector, congruent, centre/angle/direction, vector, sense — underpins describing transformations accurately before performing them.

checkQuestion: Give the child a scalene, clearly-handed shape (an 'F' or a flag) drawn on a four-quadrant grid, with tracing paper available. Ask them to: (a) reflect it in the line y = x and write the image coordinates; (b) rotate the ORIGINAL shape 90° clockwise about the point (0,0) and describe what they did; (c) translate the original by the vector '4 right, 3 down', then tell you whether the lengths and angles have changed and how they know. Watch whether they reverse the shape's sense for the reflection but NOT the rotation, whether they specify a centre and a direction for the rotation, and whether they CHECK congruence rather than assuming it.
checkAnswer: For (a) the image is the mirror across y=x with each point's coordinates swapped (e.g. (1,4)→(4,1)) and the shape's sense reversed. For (b) they pin (0,0), turn 90° clockwise, and describe it as 'a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin' — the shape's sense is unchanged. For (c) they shift every point 4 right and 3 down, and say lengths and angles are unchanged because the transformation is rigid — the image is congruent to the object, confirmable with tracing paper.
